title: Business Division — 18-Month Tool-First Curriculum (2026)
description: Six modules of 12 weeks (72 Saturdays, 144 guided learning hours). Every Saturday each learner opens a tool, performs a task, produces an output and demonstrates what they have learnt: 20 minutes demonstration, 60 minutes guided practice, 25 minutes independent assignment, 15 minutes demonstration, feedback and submission. Google Workspace first; specialist tools (Looker Studio, Manager.io, Canva, Trello, draw.io, Airtable, Make, ChatGPT) only where they solve a specific problem. Every lesson carries an 'AI, used well' strand: AI explains, suggests and challenges; the learner checks and decides. Modules 1–2 are Year 1, 3–4 Year 2, 5–6 Year 3, so members move on by mastery.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 1 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Drive**

## Why it matters

A file you cannot find is a file you do not have. Businesses lose hours to messy folders. Good structure: **few top-level folders, clear names, dates first** so files sort by time. Share with the least access needed (Viewer before Editor).

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a business folder system with properly named files and subfolders.

**Deliverable:** A shared folder for a pretend business (e.g. *Ada's Bakery*) with sub-folders Admin, Finance, Sales, Marketing, Operations — every file named `YYYY-MM-DD_topic_v1`.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to *suggest* a folder structure for a small shop — then compare it with yours and keep only what fits. You decide the names; the AI only proposes.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- At least five sub-folders with clear names
- Three files renamed to the naming pattern
- The folder shared with the instructor as Viewer

## Understand it

A business's files are its memory. When files are scattered across phones, WhatsApp chats and desktops with names like *Document (3).docx*, nobody can find anything — and when someone leaves, their knowledge leaves too. A **folder system** with **naming rules** fixes that.

**Design the structure first, on paper.** Most small businesses need a handful of top-level folders, numbered so they always sort in the same order:

- `01 Admin` — registration documents, policies, contacts
- `02 Finance` — budgets, invoices, receipts, bank statements (subfolders by year)
- `03 Customers` — lists, feedback, orders
- `04 Marketing` — logos, photos, posters
- `05 Projects` — one subfolder per project
- `99 Archive` — finished or old material

Keep it **shallow** — three levels deep is plenty. Deeper trees hide things.

**Name files so they sort and explain themselves:**

- **Date first, as YYYY-MM-DD** (`2026-03-14`) — sorts in time order automatically.
- **Then what it is**: `2026-03-14_invoice_Adebayo-Stores.pdf`
- **No spaces or special characters** (`/ \ : * ? " < > |`) — use hyphens or underscores.
- **Versions** at the end: `_v2`, `_final` (only one "final").

**In Google Drive:** *New → Folder* to create; drag files in or right-click → *Organise → Move*; right-click → *Rename*. **Colour** top-level folders and **star** the ones you use daily. Use the search bar with filters (type, owner, date modified) — good names make search work.

Write the naming rule into a short `README` doc in the top folder, so everyone follows it.

## Key words

- **Folder structure:** the planned arrangement of folders and subfolders
- **Naming convention:** an agreed rule for naming files
- **ISO date:** YYYY-MM-DD, which sorts correctly
- **Archive:** where finished or old files are kept

## Read and watch

- [Organise your files in Google Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/2375091) — Google Drive Help
- [File naming conventions](https://datamanagement.hms.harvard.edu/plan-design/file-naming-conventions) — Harvard Medical School Data Management
- [How to use Google Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/2424384) — Google Drive Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Create a business folder system with properly named files and subfolders. A shared folder for a pretend business (e.g. *Ada's Bakery*) with sub-folders Admin, Finance, Sales, Marketing, Operations — every file named `YYYY-MM-DD_topic_v1`.

> No tool without a deliverable. No mastery by attendance. No unnecessary software.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 2 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Docs**

## Why it matters

Professional documents use **styles**, not manual formatting: headings make a document scannable and build an automatic outline. Keep sentences short, put the most important fact first, and proofread before sharing.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Write a professional business introduction and format it correctly.

**Deliverable:** A one-page introduction to your business: name, what it sells, who it serves, why it is different, and contact details.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Uses Heading 1, Heading 2 and Normal text styles — no manual big fonts
- Short paragraphs, one idea each
- Spelling and grammar checked (Tools → Spelling and grammar)

## Understand it

A **business introduction** (a short company profile) tells a reader who you are, what you do, for whom, and why they should trust you — in one page. It goes to partners, customers, banks and grant panels, and it is judged in seconds: content first, then how professional it looks.

**What to include:**

1. **Name and one-line description** — "Ada's Kitchen prepares fresh lunch packs for offices in Ikeja."
2. **The problem you solve** and **for whom**.
3. **What you offer** — products or services, briefly.
4. **Why you** — experience, quality, location, price, track record (with numbers: "serving 120 customers weekly since 2024").
5. **Contact details** — phone, email, address, social handle.

**Formatting it correctly in Google Docs:**

- Use **styles**, not manual bold-and-bigger: select a line → the style menu (*Normal text*) → *Title*, *Heading 1*, *Heading 2*. Styles keep formatting consistent and build an automatic outline (*View → Show outline*) and table of contents.
- **One or two fonts** at most; body text 11–12 pt; generous line spacing (*Format → Line & paragraph spacing*, 1.15).
- **Short paragraphs** and **bullet points** for lists.
- **Margins** at least 2 cm; **align left** (justified text creates uneven gaps).
- A **header** or **footer** with the business name (*Insert → Headers & footers*).
- Check with *Tools → Spelling and grammar*, and read it aloud.

Export as PDF (*File → Download → PDF*) to send — it looks the same on every device.

## Key words

- **Company profile:** a short document introducing a business
- **Paragraph style:** a saved format such as Heading 1 applied consistently
- **Header / footer:** text repeated at the top / bottom of every page

## Read and watch

- [How to use Google Docs](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/7068618) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Add a title, heading or table of contents](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/116338) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Plain language guidelines](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/) — plainlanguage.gov

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Write a professional business introduction and format it correctly. A one-page introduction to your business: name, what it sells, who it serves, why it is different, and contact details.

> No tool without a deliverable. No mastery by attendance. No unnecessary software.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 3 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Docs**

## Why it matters

A **formal letter** follows a fixed layout so it is taken seriously. A **report** answers a question with evidence: *summary first*, then findings, then what to do. Use a table for numbers.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Prepare a formal business letter and a one-page report.

**Deliverable:** A formal letter to a supplier requesting a price list, and a one-page report on last week's (sample) sales.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- The letter has sender address, date, recipient, subject line, salutation, body and sign-off
- The report has a title, summary, findings and a recommendation
- Both fit on one page each

## Understand it

Formal letters and short reports are how organisations make requests, confirm agreements and keep records. Their layouts are conventions — readers expect information in particular places, so following them makes you look professional and helps the reader.

**A formal business letter (block format — everything aligned left):**

1. **Your letterhead** — business name, address, phone, email.
2. **Date** — written in full: 14 March 2026.
3. **Recipient** — name, title, organisation, address.
4. **Reference line** (optional) — "Ref: Venue booking, 28 March".
5. **Salutation** — "Dear Mrs Okafor," (or "Dear Sir/Madam," if you truly do not know the name).
6. **Subject line in bold** — what the letter is about.
7. **Body** — opening paragraph with the purpose; middle paragraph(s) with details; closing paragraph with the action required and by when.
8. **Close** — "Yours sincerely," (when you named the person) or "Yours faithfully," (Sir/Madam); signature; full name; title.

**A one-page report:**

- **Title** and date, author.
- **Summary** — the key finding and recommendation in two or three sentences, first.
- **Background** — why the report was written.
- **Findings** — what you found, with numbers, under clear headings; a small table if useful.
- **Recommendations** — numbered, specific actions.

In Docs: use **headings** (*Format → Paragraph styles*), insert a **table** (*Insert → Table*), and add **page numbers** (*Insert → Page numbers*). Keep to one page by cutting words, not by shrinking the font.

## Key words

- **Block format:** a letter layout with every part aligned left
- **Salutation:** the greeting, e.g. 'Dear Mrs Okafor'
- **Executive summary:** the key points of a report, placed first
- **Recommendation:** a specific action the report proposes

## Read and watch

- [Use headers, footers, page numbers and footnotes](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/86629) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Add and edit tables](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/1696711) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Plain language guidelines](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/) — plainlanguage.gov

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Prepare a formal business letter and a one-page report. A formal letter to a supplier requesting a price list, and a one-page report on last week's (sample) sales.

> No tool without a deliverable. No mastery by attendance. No unnecessary software.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 4 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A spreadsheet is a grid of **cells** (A1, B2…). Data goes in rows — one row per item — and columns hold one kind of fact each. Let formulas do the arithmetic: `=C2*D2` then fill down. Freeze the header (View → Freeze → 1 row).

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create an inventory register with products, quantities and prices.

**Deliverable:** An inventory register with columns Product, Category, Quantity, Unit price and Stock value, for at least 15 products.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Header row frozen and bold
- Stock value = Quantity × Unit price by formula, not typed
- Prices formatted as currency (₦)

## Understand it

An **inventory register** lists every product a business holds: what it is, how many, and what it is worth. Without it, owners do not notice theft, waste or slow-moving stock, and they run out of best-sellers.

**Build it as a proper table:**

| Product | Category | Quantity | Unit price (₦) | Stock value (₦) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rice 50kg | Grains | 12 | 78,000 | `=C2*D2` |

- **Row 1 is the header** — one label per column. Make it bold and **freeze** it (*View → Freeze → 1 row*) so it stays visible when you scroll.
- **One row per product, one kind of fact per column.** Never merge cells or leave blank rows inside the table — they break sorting and formulas.
- **Stock value by formula**, not typed: in E2 type `=C2*D2`, press Enter, then drag the small square at the cell's bottom-right corner (the **fill handle**) down — the formula adjusts for each row (`=C3*D3`, `=C4*D4`).
- **Total** at the bottom: `=SUM(E2:E16)`.
- **Currency format**: select the price and value columns → *Format → Number → Currency* (or a custom ₦ format).
- Optional: a **Category** dropdown via *Data → Data validation*, so "Grains" is never typed as "grain" or "Grain ".

**Why formulas, not typed totals:** change a quantity and every total updates instantly — and there are no arithmetic mistakes.

Count the real stock regularly (a **stock-take**) and compare with the register; differences reveal waste or loss.

## Key words

- **Inventory register:** a list of stock with quantities and values
- **Fill handle:** the corner square used to copy a formula down
- **Freeze row:** keep the header visible while scrolling
- **Stock-take:** physically counting stock to check records

## Read and watch

- [How to use Google Sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6000292) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [SUM function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093669) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Data validation](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/186103) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

Create an inventory register with products, quantities and prices. An inventory register with columns Product, Category, Quantity, Unit price and Stock value, for at least 15 products.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 5 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Functions summarise data: `=SUM(B2:B31)`, `=AVERAGE(B2:B31)`, `=MIN(…)`, `=MAX(…)`. A **range** like B2:B31 means every cell from B2 to B31. Numbers alone are not insight — always say what they mean.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Use SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX to analyse sample figures.

**Deliverable:** An analysis block under a sheet of 30 days of sample sales: total, average, best day and worst day.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Uses SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX on the right ranges
- Each result has a clear label
- One sentence explaining what the numbers show

## Understand it

Four functions answer the first questions anyone asks of a column of numbers:

- `=SUM(B2:B31)` — the **total**. "How much did we sell this month?"
- `=AVERAGE(B2:B31)` — the **mean** (total ÷ count). "What is a typical day?"
- `=MIN(B2:B31)` — the **smallest** value. "What was our worst day?"
- `=MAX(B2:B31)` — the **largest** value. "What was our best day?"

**How a function is written:** an equals sign, the function name, and the **range** in brackets. `B2:B31` means "every cell from B2 to B31". Click and drag over the cells instead of typing the range, to avoid mistakes. Add `=COUNT(B2:B31)` to see how many numbers there are.

**Reading the results like an analyst:**

- If **MAX** is far above the **AVERAGE**, find out what happened that day — a big order? A market day? An event you could repeat?
- If **MIN** is zero, was the shop closed, or was a sale not recorded?
- **The average can mislead** when a few extreme values pull it. Average sales of ₦40,000 could mean every day was ₦40,000 — or most days ₦20,000 and two huge days. `=MEDIAN(...)` (the middle value) is often a better "typical day".

**Blank vs zero:** these functions ignore empty cells but include zeros. A missing record and a zero-sales day are different facts — record them differently.

Put a small **summary block** beside the data (labels: Total, Average, Lowest, Highest) so anyone can read the answers at a glance.

## Key words

- **Function:** a built-in formula such as SUM or AVERAGE
- **Range:** a block of cells, e.g. B2:B31
- **Mean (average):** total divided by count
- **Median:** the middle value when sorted

## Read and watch

- [AVERAGE function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093615) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [MAX function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3094013) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [MIN function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3094017) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.

> **Programme week 6 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Money in, money out. A running balance is `=previous balance + income − expense`. Small businesses fail when they cannot see cash leaving. Record every transaction on the day it happens.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Build a daily income and expenditure tracker.

**Deliverable:** A tracker with Date, Description, Income, Expense and Running balance for two weeks of sample entries.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Running balance calculated by formula
- Totals for income and expenses
- A note of the day with the biggest expense

## Understand it

A **daily income and expenditure tracker** is the simplest financial record a business can keep — and the one most small businesses skip. It answers: *how much came in, how much went out, and what is left?*

**Columns:**

| Date | Description | Category | Money in (₦) | Money out (₦) | Balance (₦) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Date** — formatted as a date (*Format → Number → Date*), so it sorts correctly.
- **Description** — specific: "Sold 12 lunch packs", "Bought 2 crates of eggs".
- **Category** — a dropdown (*Data → Data validation → Dropdown*): Sales, Stock, Transport, Rent, Utilities, Wages, Other. Consistent categories make totals possible later.
- **Money in** and **Money out** in separate columns — never one column with minus signs; it is easier to read and to total.
- **Running balance**: the first row is the opening balance; then in F3: `=F2+D3-E3`, filled down. Each row shows how much is left after that transaction.

**Totals:** `=SUM(D:D)` for income, `=SUM(E:E)` for spending; profit = income − spending.

**By category:** `=SUMIF(C:C,"Transport",E:E)` adds up all Transport spending — you will often be surprised where the money goes.

**Rules that make it trustworthy:** record **every day**, the same day; keep receipts (photograph them into a Drive folder); **keep business and personal money separate**; and check the balance against the cash box and bank regularly.

## Key words

- **Income:** money coming into the business
- **Expenditure:** money going out
- **Running balance:** the amount left after each transaction
- **Category:** a group used to total similar transactions

## Read and watch

- [SUMIF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093583) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Data validation](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/186103) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Small business support](https://www.smedan.gov.ng/) — SMEDAN (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria)

- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

> **Programme week 7 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Forms**

## Why it matters

Surveys turn opinions into data. Ask **one thing per question**, keep it neutral (no leading questions), and do not collect personal data you do not need. Link responses to a sheet (Responses → Link to Sheets).

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a customer survey and collect sample responses.

**Deliverable:** A 6–8 question customer survey (multiple choice, scale and one short answer) with at least 10 sample responses.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to suggest five survey questions, then remove any that are leading, personal or confusing. Good questions are short, neutral and answerable.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- A clear title and one-line purpose
- Question types fit the question (scale for satisfaction, choice for categories)
- Responses linked to a Google Sheet

## Understand it

A **customer survey** collects opinions from many people quickly — but only if it is short, clear and asks the right questions. Bad questions give useless or misleading answers.

**Start from the decision.** What will you decide with the results? ("Whether to open on Sundays", "Which new product to stock".) Ask only questions that help that decision. Aim for **under 10 questions, under 3 minutes**.

**Choose the right question type in Google Forms:**

- **Multiple choice** — one answer from a list ("How often do you buy from us?").
- **Checkboxes** — several answers allowed ("Which days suit you?").
- **Linear scale** — 1 to 5 ratings ("How satisfied are you?").
- **Dropdown** — long lists (area, age group).
- **Short answer / paragraph** — open comments; use sparingly — they take longer to answer and to analyse.

**Write good questions:**

- **One thing per question** — not "Was our food tasty and affordable?" (what if it was tasty but expensive?).
- **Neutral wording** — not "How much did you love our new menu?"
- **Answer options that cover everything** and do not overlap — include "Other" or "Not sure".
- **Ask about behaviour** ("How many times did you buy last month?") rather than predictions.

**Settings:** mark essential questions **Required**; use *Settings → Responses* to decide whether to collect emails (only if you need them — data minimisation). Collect **no more personal data than you need**.

Preview it, test it on two people, fix confusing questions, then share the link.

## Key words

- **Survey:** a set of questions sent to many people
- **Leading question:** a question that pushes towards an answer
- **Linear scale:** a numbered rating question, e.g. 1–5
- **Required question:** one that must be answered to submit

## Read and watch

- [Create a form](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6281888) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Choose a type of question for your form](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/7322334) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Publish and share your form](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/2839588) — Google Docs Editors Help

**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 8 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Sorting puts rows in order; **filters** show only the rows you want without deleting others. `=COUNTIF(C2:C50,"Very satisfied")` counts answers. Findings should be facts from the data, not guesses.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Sort, filter and analyse survey results.

**Deliverable:** An analysis of last week's survey: sorted, filtered views and a short findings box with three key results.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Uses Sort and a Filter view
- Counts answers with COUNTIF
- Three findings written in plain language

## Understand it

Survey responses arrive as rows in a spreadsheet — one row per person, one column per question. **Sorting**, **filtering** and **counting** turn those rows into answers.

**Link the form to Sheets:** in Google Forms, *Responses → Link to Sheets*. New answers appear automatically.

**Before analysing, protect the original:** work on a **copy** of the response sheet (right-click the tab → *Duplicate*), so the raw data stays untouched.

**Sort** — *Data → Sort range* (tick "Data has header row"), choose a column, A→Z or Z→A. Sorting by rating brings the unhappy customers together so you can read their comments.

**Filter** — *Data → Create a filter*. Small icons appear in the header; click one to show only certain values (e.g. only people from Yaba). The other rows are hidden, not deleted. **Filter views** let several people filter without disturbing each other.

**Count answers:**

- `=COUNTIF(C:C,"Weekly")` — how many chose "Weekly".
- `=COUNTA(C2:C)` — how many responses in total.
- Percentage: count ÷ total, formatted as % (*Format → Number → Percent*).
- `=AVERAGE(D2:D)` — the average rating.

**Pivot tables** (*Insert → Pivot table*) summarise in a few clicks: rows = area, values = COUNTA of responses — a count per area without any formulas.

**Report findings honestly:** say how many people answered. "80% preferred Saturdays" from 5 people is not the same as from 200.

## Key words

- **Sort:** reorder rows by a column's values
- **Filter:** show only rows that match a condition
- **COUNTIF:** count cells that meet a condition
- **Pivot table:** a summary table that groups and counts data

## Read and watch

- [Sort and filter your data](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3540681) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [COUNTIF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093480) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Create and use pivot tables](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/1272900) — Google Docs Editors Help

> **Programme week 9 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Slides**

## Why it matters

Slides support the speaker; they are not a document. Use **big headlines, few words and one visual per slide**. Insert a chart from Sheets (Insert → Chart → From Sheets) so it updates with your data.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Develop a five-slide business presentation.

**Deliverable:** A five-slide deck: title, the problem, your solution, evidence (a chart from your survey), and the ask / next step.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- One idea per slide, few words
- At least one chart taken from your sheet
- Presented in under three minutes

## Understand it

A short presentation is often how a business is judged — by a client, a panel, a manager. Five slides force you to keep only what matters.

**A five-slide structure that works:**

1. **Title** — business name, a one-line description, your name.
2. **The problem** — who has it, with one real example or number.
3. **The solution** — what you offer, with a photo of the product or service.
4. **Evidence and numbers** — customers, sales, survey results, costs — one clear chart beats a table of figures.
5. **The ask or next step** — what you want from the audience, and contact details.

**Design principles:**

- **One idea per slide.** The headline states the point ("Customers want Saturday delivery"), not just the topic ("Survey").
- **Few words** — slides support what you say; they are not a script. If the audience is reading, they are not listening.
- **Large text** — at least 24 pt; titles bigger.
- **High contrast** — dark text on light background or the reverse; never yellow on white.
- **Consistent layout** — use the **theme** and **layouts** (*Slide → Change theme*, *Slide → Apply layout*) rather than placing boxes by hand.
- **Real images**, not clip art; check you have the right to use them.

**In Google Slides:** *Slide → New slide* (Ctrl+M); insert charts from Sheets (*Insert → Chart → From Sheets*) so they update; add **speaker notes** below each slide for your talking points; present with *Slideshow*.

Rehearse aloud with a timer.

## Key words

- **Slide layout:** a preset arrangement of title and content
- **Theme:** consistent fonts and colours across slides
- **Speaker notes:** notes for the presenter, hidden from the audience
- **Headline:** a slide title that states the point

## Read and watch

- [Add, delete and organise slides](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/1694830) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [How to make a great presentation](https://www.ted.com/playlists/574/how_to_make_a_great_presentation) — TED
- [Understanding minimum contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

> **Programme week 10 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Calendar**

## Why it matters

Plans fail in time, not in ideas. A calendar makes deadlines visible. Use colours for event types, add the agenda in the description, and set reminders a day before deadlines.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Schedule a project with deadlines, meetings and reminders.

**Deliverable:** A project calendar for a four-week product launch: milestones, two team meetings, deadlines and reminders.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to list the steps of your project in order, then check each date is realistic for your team before it goes in the calendar.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- At least six events with clear titles
- Reminders set on deadlines
- One meeting with a guest invited and an agenda in the description

## Understand it

A project lives or dies by its **dates**. A shared calendar makes deadlines and meetings visible to everyone, and reminders mean nobody relies on memory.

**Plan backwards from the deadline.** If the event is on 28 March: invitations must go by 14 March; the venue must be confirmed by 7 March; the budget approved by 3 March. Each becomes a calendar entry with its owner.

**In Google Calendar:**

- **Create an event** — click a time slot (or *Create*). Add a **clear title** ("Venue confirmed — Tunde"), the time, location, and a **description** with links to the relevant documents.
- **All-day events** for deadlines; timed events for meetings.
- **Invite people** — *Add guests*; they receive the invitation and can accept or decline. Use the *Find a time* view to see when everyone is free.
- **Reminders (notifications)** — add one a few days before for big deadlines and one 30 minutes before meetings.
- **Recurring events** — *Does not repeat → Weekly on Saturday* for regular meetings.
- **A separate project calendar** (*Other calendars → + → Create new calendar*), shared with the team, keeps project dates apart from personal ones and can be shown or hidden.
- **Colours** by type — deadlines red, meetings blue.

**Good meeting entries** include the purpose and an agenda link, so people arrive prepared.

Review the project calendar at the start of every week: what is due, who is responsible, what is at risk?

## Key words

- **Deadline:** the date by which something must be done
- **Backward planning:** scheduling from the end date back to today
- **Recurring event:** an event that repeats on a schedule
- **Shared calendar:** a calendar several people can view or edit

## Read and watch

- [Create an event](https://support.google.com/calendar/answer/72143) — Google Calendar Help
- [Invite people to your event](https://support.google.com/calendar/answer/37161) — Google Calendar Help

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 11 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Drive + Docs**

## Why it matters

Collaboration is a skill. Use **Suggesting mode** to propose edits, **comments** to discuss, and @mention people to assign actions. Version history shows who changed what — respect other people's work.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Collaborate on a shared project folder and report.

**Deliverable:** A team folder and a shared report written by three people, using comments, suggestions and version history.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Each team member has written a section
- At least three comments resolved
- Version history shows everyone's contributions

## Understand it

Collaboration tools let a team work on **one copy** of a document instead of emailing versions back and forth ("report_final_v3_REAL.docx"). They also introduce new responsibilities: who can see, who can change, and what happened when.

**Sharing with the right access** (*Share* button):

- **Viewer** — can read only.
- **Commenter** — can read and add comments and suggestions.
- **Editor** — can change everything (and, by default, share it further).

Give the **least access needed**. Share with named people rather than "Anyone with the link" for anything internal or sensitive. A shared **folder** passes its permissions to everything inside it.

**Working together in Docs:**

- **Comments** (*Insert → Comment*, or Ctrl+Alt+M) — discuss a passage without changing it. Type `@name` to assign a comment as an **action item** to a person; they get notified. **Resolve** comments when done.
- **Suggesting mode** (the pencil icon, top right → *Suggesting*) — edits appear as tracked suggestions the owner can accept or reject. Use it when editing someone else's writing.
- **Version history** (*File → Version history → See version history*) — see who changed what and when, and restore an earlier version. Name important versions ("Sent to client 14 March").

**Agree ground rules:** who owns the document, who writes which section, the deadline for comments, and who makes final decisions. Assign sections by name in the document itself.

## Key words

- **Access level:** viewer, commenter or editor
- **Suggesting mode:** edits shown as suggestions to accept or reject
- **Version history:** a record of every change and who made it
- **Action item:** a comment assigned to a person to act on

## Read and watch

- [Share and manage access to files](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/2494822) — Google Drive Help
- [Use comments and action items](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/65129) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Find what's changed in a file](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/190843) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Collaborate on a shared project folder and report. A team folder and a shared report written by three people, using comments, suggestions and version history.

> No tool without a deliverable. No mastery by attendance. No unnecessary software.

> **Programme week 12 of 72 · Module 1: Digital Productivity and Business Basics.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Integrated challenge**

## Why it matters

This is Module 1's demonstration of mastery. A **portfolio** proves skill with evidence. Choose your best version of each piece, fix last week's feedback, and explain what you learned and how you would use it in a real business.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Produce and present a complete digital business portfolio.

**Deliverable:** A portfolio folder with your best work from weeks 1–11 and a three-minute presentation of it.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Folder system, a document, a sheet with formulas, a form with results, a deck and a calendar — all present and named
- A one-page index linking to each item
- Presentation explains what each item shows you can do

## Understand it

The **digital business portfolio** brings together everything in Module 1 into one organised, shareable package — the kind of evidence an employer, client or funder wants to see.

**What it should contain (in your Drive folder system from week 1):**

1. **Business introduction** (week 2) — formatted with styles, exported as PDF.
2. **Formal letter and one-page report** (week 3).
3. **Inventory register** (week 4) with formulas and totals.
4. **Sales analysis** (week 5) with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX.
5. **Income and expenditure tracker** (week 6) with a running balance.
6. **Customer survey and its results** (weeks 7–8), with counts and one chart.
7. **Five-slide presentation** (week 9).
8. **Project calendar** screenshot or link (week 10).
9. **Shared report** showing comments and version history (week 11).

**Quality checks before presenting:**

- **Consistent file names** following your naming rule.
- **Formulas, not typed numbers** — click a few cells to check.
- **Sharing set correctly** — can the assessor open everything? Test the link in a private/incognito window.
- **A front page** — a README or index doc listing each item with a link and one line describing it.

**Presenting it:** walk through the portfolio in five minutes: what each item is, which tool, and **one decision you made** and why (a column you added, a question you changed). Assessors look for understanding, not just finished files.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** an organised collection of work as evidence of skill
- **Index document:** a front page listing and linking every item
- **Incognito check:** testing a link while signed out to confirm access

## Read and watch

- [Organise your files in Google Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/2375091) — Google Drive Help
- [Google Docs training and help](https://support.google.com/a/users/answer/9282664) — Google Workspace Learning Center

Produce and present a complete digital business portfolio. A portfolio folder with your best work from weeks 1–11 and a three-minute presentation of it.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 13 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A **relative** reference (B2) changes when you fill down; an **absolute** one ($B$1) does not — use it for a fixed rate. **Data validation** stops wrong entries; **conditional formatting** makes problems visible.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Master cell references, formatting and data validation.

**Deliverable:** A price list using relative and absolute references ($B## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

 for a tax rate) and drop-down validation for categories.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a formula you do not understand, e.g. *"What does =SUMIF(B2:B20,\"Bread\",C2:C20) do?"* — then test it on three rows you can check by hand. A formula is only right when your hand-check agrees.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- A formula that uses an absolute reference correctly
- A drop-down list built with data validation
- Conditional formatting that highlights low stock

## Understand it

Three spreadsheet skills separate a reliable financial sheet from a fragile one: **cell references**, **number formatting** and **data validation**.

**Relative vs absolute references:**

- A normal reference like `B2` is **relative**: copy `=B2*C2` down one row and it becomes `=B3*C3`. That is usually what you want.
- Sometimes a formula must always point to **one fixed cell** — a VAT rate in `F1`, an exchange rate, a commission percentage. Write it as **`$F$1`** — the dollar signs **lock** the column and row. `=B2*$F$1` copied down becomes `=B3*$F$1`.
- **Mixed references**: `$F1` locks the column only; `F$1` locks the row only — useful in tables that copy both across and down.
- Press **F4** (or Fn+F4) while the cursor is in a reference to cycle through the options.

**Formatting** changes how a number **looks**, not its value: *Format → Number* → Currency, Percent, Date, Number with 2 decimals. Format whole columns consistently. Never type "₦5,000" as text — type 5000 and format it, or formulas cannot use it.

**Data validation** stops bad data **before** it gets in (*Data → Data validation*):

- **Dropdown** from a list (Paid / Unpaid / Partly paid).
- **Number between** limits (quantity 0–1000).
- **Date** rules (not in the future).
- Set it to **reject input** with a helpful message, rather than just warning.

**Protect** formula columns and headers (*Data → Protect sheets and ranges*) so they are not typed over.

## Key words

- **Relative reference:** a reference that shifts when copied
- **Absolute reference:** a locked reference like $F$1
- **Number format:** how a value is displayed — currency, %, date
- **Data validation:** rules that limit what can be entered

## Read and watch

- [Data validation](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/186103) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Protect, hide and edit sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/1218656) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Conditional formatting rules](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Master cell references, formatting and data validation. A price list using relative and absolute references ($B$1 for a tax rate) and drop-down validation for categories.

> No tool without a deliverable. No mastery by attendance. No unnecessary software.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 14 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Revenue is not profit. **Gross profit** is what is left after the cost of what you sold; **net profit** is what is left after every expense. Margin % = profit ÷ revenue.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Calculate sales, costs, gross profit and net profit.

**Deliverable:** A profit sheet for a month of sample sales: revenue, cost of goods, gross profit, expenses and net profit.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Gross profit = revenue − cost of goods
- Net profit = gross profit − expenses
- Profit margins shown as percentages

## Understand it

Two profit figures tell different stories, and every business owner should know both.

**Sales (revenue)** — total money from selling: quantity × price.

**Cost of sales (cost of goods sold)** — the **direct** cost of the items sold: stock bought for resale, ingredients, packaging.

**Gross profit = Sales − Cost of sales.** It shows whether the **product itself** makes money.

**Operating expenses (overheads)** — the costs of running the business, whatever you sell: rent, salaries, electricity, fuel, data, marketing, transport.

**Net profit = Gross profit − Operating expenses.** It shows whether the **business as a whole** makes money.

**Margins** make them comparable across months and businesses:

- **Gross margin %** = Gross profit ÷ Sales × 100.
- **Net margin %** = Net profit ÷ Sales × 100.

**Example:** sales ₦600,000; cost of sales ₦360,000 → gross profit ₦240,000 (40%). Expenses ₦180,000 → net profit ₦60,000 (10%).

**What they reveal:**

- **Low gross margin** → prices too low or buying costs too high.
- **Good gross margin but low net** → overheads too high.

**In Sheets:** a small **profit and loss** table — Sales, Cost of sales, Gross profit (formula), each expense line, Total expenses (`=SUM`), Net profit (formula), and the two margins formatted as %. Lay months across the columns to see the trend.

## Key words

- **Gross profit:** sales minus the direct cost of goods sold
- **Net profit:** gross profit minus all operating expenses
- **Margin:** profit as a percentage of sales
- **Profit and loss (P&L):** a statement of income, costs and profit for a period

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Business](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpsvr82) — BBC Bitesize
- [SUM function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093669) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

Calculate sales, costs, gross profit and net profit. A profit sheet for a month of sample sales: revenue, cost of goods, gross profit, expenses and net profit.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 15 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

`=IF(D2>50000,"Large","Standard")` makes a decision. `=COUNTIF(range,"Bread")` counts; `=SUMIF(range,"Bread",sum_range)` adds. Always hand-check one result.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Use IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF in business records.

**Deliverable:** A sales record that flags large orders with IF, counts orders per product and totals sales per product.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- An IF formula with a clear rule
- COUNTIF and SUMIF used for at least two products
- Results labelled and checked by hand on one product

## Understand it

Three functions let a spreadsheet make **decisions** and **conditional totals** — the start of real business analysis.

**IF** — choose a result based on a test:

`=IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false)`

- `=IF(C2>=D2, "Paid", "Owing")` — compares amount paid (C2) with amount due (D2).
- `=IF(E2<5, "Reorder", "OK")` — stock alert.
- `=IF(B2>100000, B2*0.05, 0)` — 5% bonus on sales over ₦100,000.
- Comparison operators: `=`, `<>` (not equal), `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`. Text must be in "quotes".

**COUNTIF** — count cells that meet a condition:

- `=COUNTIF(F:F, "Owing")` — how many customers owe money.
- `=COUNTIF(B:B, ">50000")` — how many sales above ₦50,000 (the condition in quotes).

**SUMIF** — add values where a condition is met:

`=SUMIF(range_to_check, condition, range_to_add)`

- `=SUMIF(C:C, "Transport", E:E)` — total spent on transport.
- `=SUMIF(F:F, "Owing", D:D)` — total amount owed.

**COUNTIFS / SUMIFS** take several conditions: `=SUMIFS(E:E, C:C, "Transport", A:A, ">="&DATE(2026,3,1))` — transport since 1 March.

**Tip:** put conditions in cells (e.g. the category in H1) and refer to them: `=SUMIF(C:C, H1, E:E)`. Change H1 and the total updates — a simple interactive report. Combine with **conditional formatting** to colour "Owing" rows red automatically.

## Key words

- **IF:** returns one value if a test is true, another if false
- **COUNTIF:** counts cells meeting a condition
- **SUMIF:** adds values where a condition is met
- **Logical test:** a comparison that is true or false

## Read and watch

- [IF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093364) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [COUNTIF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093480) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [SUMIF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093583) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

Use IF, COUNTIF and SUMIF in business records. A sales record that flags large orders with IF, counts orders per product and totals sales per product.

> **Programme week 16 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A **budget** is a plan for money; tracking actuals against it shows where the plan was wrong. Overspends are information, not failure — act on them.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Build a monthly budget and expense tracker.

**Deliverable:** A budget with planned and actual amounts per category for one month, and the difference.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Planned vs actual for at least eight categories
- Difference column with conditional formatting
- A note on the biggest overspend and what to do

## Understand it

A **budget** is a plan for money: what you expect to earn and spend over a period. An **expense tracker** records what actually happens. Comparing the two each month is how businesses (and households) stay in control.

**Build the budget sheet:**

| Category | Budget (₦) | Actual (₦) | Difference (₦) | % used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rent | 50,000 | `=SUMIF(...)` | `=B2-C2` | `=C2/B2` |

- **Income** lines at the top (sales, grants, contributions), **expense** lines below, grouped by category.
- **Actual** pulled automatically from the expense tracker with **SUMIF** by category — no retyping.
- **Difference** = budget − actual. Positive = under budget; negative = overspent.
- **% used** formatted as percent. Use **conditional formatting** (*Format → Conditional formatting*) to turn cells red above 100% and amber above 80%.

**The expense tracker** (separate tab): Date, Description, Category (dropdown — **the same category names** as the budget, or SUMIF will miss them), Amount, Payment method, Receipt link.

**Budgeting habits:**

- **Base the budget on evidence** — last months' actual spending — not hopes.
- Include **irregular costs** (repairs, annual registration, festive season) by setting aside a monthly amount.
- Keep a **contingency** (5–10%) for the unexpected.
- **Review monthly**: where did you overspend, and why? Adjust next month's budget or behaviour.

A budget that is never compared with actuals is just a wish list.

## Key words

- **Budget:** a plan of expected income and spending
- **Actual:** what was really earned or spent
- **Variance:** the difference between budget and actual
- **Contingency:** money set aside for the unexpected

## Read and watch

- [SUMIF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093583) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Conditional formatting rules](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

> **Programme week 17 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Running out loses sales; overstocking ties up cash. A **reorder level** is the quantity at which you buy more. Let the sheet tell you what to reorder.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create an inventory and stock-reorder tracker.

**Deliverable:** An inventory sheet that flags any product below its reorder level.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a formula you do not understand, e.g. *"What does =SUMIF(B2:B20,\"Bread\",C2:C20) do?"* — then test it on three rows you can check by hand. A formula is only right when your hand-check agrees.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Reorder level column per product
- IF or conditional formatting flags items to reorder
- A list of items to reorder this week

## Understand it

Running out of a best-seller loses sales; holding too much stock ties up cash and risks spoilage. A **stock-reorder tracker** tells you **what to buy, and when**.

**Columns:**

| Item | Opening stock | Received | Sold/used | Closing stock | Reorder level | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Closing stock** = Opening + Received − Sold: `=B2+C2-D2`.
- **Reorder level** — the quantity at which you must order more. Work it out:
  - **Reorder level = average daily usage × lead time (days) + safety stock**.
  - If you sell 10 a day, the supplier takes 3 days to deliver, and you keep 10 spare: 10 × 3 + 10 = **40**. When stock falls to 40, order.
- **Status** with IF: `=IF(E2<=F2, "REORDER", "OK")`.
- **Conditional formatting** colours REORDER rows red so they jump out.
- **Reorder quantity** — how much to order: enough to last until the next normal order, considering storage space, cash, shelf life and bulk discounts.

**Keeping it accurate:**

- Record **every** receipt and sale — a missed entry makes the whole sheet wrong.
- **Stock-take** regularly — count physically and compare with the sheet. Differences (**shrinkage**) mean theft, damage, spoilage or recording errors; investigate them.
- For perishables, track **expiry dates** and sell oldest first (**FIFO** — first in, first out).

A `COUNTIF(G:G, "REORDER")` cell at the top tells the manager at a glance how many items need ordering today.

## Key words

- **Reorder level:** the stock quantity that triggers a new order
- **Lead time:** the time between ordering and receiving
- **Safety stock:** extra stock kept for delays or demand spikes
- **FIFO:** first in, first out — sell the oldest stock first

## Read and watch

- [IF function](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3093364) — Google Docs Editors Help
- [Conditional formatting rules](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) — Google Docs Editors Help

> **Programme week 18 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A **cashbook** records every naira in and out. **Reconciling** compares it with the bank statement line by line — differences are errors or timing (a cheque not yet cleared).

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Prepare a cashbook and reconcile simulated transactions.

**Deliverable:** A cashbook for a month of simulated transactions, reconciled against a sample bank statement.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Opening balance, receipts, payments, closing balance
- Every difference with the statement explained
- Closing balance matches after reconciliation

## Understand it

A **cashbook** records every movement of cash and bank money in date order. **Reconciliation** checks it against reality — the cash box count and the bank statement. Businesses that reconcile catch errors, fraud and forgotten charges early; those that do not often discover problems months too late.

**Cashbook columns:**

| Date | Details | Ref (receipt no.) | Cash in | Cash out | Bank in | Bank out | Cash balance | Bank balance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Running balances: cash balance = previous + cash in − cash out; likewise for bank.

**Reconciling with the bank statement:**

1. Put the bank statement and your cashbook side by side for the same period.
2. **Tick off** every item that appears in **both** (a checkbox column helps: *Insert → Checkbox*).
3. List what is left:
   - **In the bank but not your book** — bank charges, SMS alerts, interest, transfers you forgot to record, POS fees. **Add them to your cashbook.**
   - **In your book but not the bank yet** — cheques or transfers not yet cleared (**timing differences**). They should appear soon.
4. **Adjusted cashbook balance** should equal **bank statement balance** ± timing differences. If not, there is an error to find.

**Cash:** count the cash box at the end of each day and compare with the cash balance. A difference must be explained, not just adjusted.

Reconcile **monthly** at least — weekly for busy businesses. The person who records should ideally not be the only person who reconciles (a basic **control** against fraud).

## Key words

- **Cashbook:** a date-order record of cash and bank receipts and payments
- **Bank reconciliation:** matching your records with the bank statement
- **Timing difference:** an item recorded but not yet cleared by the bank
- **Control:** a check that prevents or detects errors and fraud

## Why it matters

Choose the chart for the question: **trend → line**, **comparison → bar**, **share → pie**. A chart without a title and an insight is decoration.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create charts from sales and customer data.

**Deliverable:** Three charts: monthly sales trend (line), sales by product (bar), customer types (pie).

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Right chart type for each question
- Clear titles and axis labels
- One insight written under each chart

## Understand it

A good chart shows in two seconds what a table takes two minutes to read. A bad chart misleads. The key is choosing the **right chart for the question**.

**Match chart to question:**

- **How does something change over time?** → **Line chart** (monthly sales).
- **How do categories compare?** → **Bar or column chart** (sales by product, customers by area). Sort bars from largest to smallest.
- **What are the parts of a whole?** → **Pie chart**, but only with **few slices (2–5)**; otherwise use a bar chart — people judge lengths far better than angles.
- **Is there a relationship between two numbers?** → **Scatter chart** (advertising spend vs sales).

**In Google Sheets:** select the data including headers → *Insert → Chart*. In the **Chart editor**: *Setup* chooses the type and data range; *Customise* changes titles, colours, axes and labels.

**Make charts honest and readable:**

- **Title says the finding**: "Sales doubled after we added delivery", not just "Sales".
- **Label axes** with units (₦, number of customers).
- **Bar charts start at zero** — a cut-off axis makes small differences look huge.
- **Remove clutter** — no 3D, no shadows, minimal gridlines.
- **Highlight** the important bar or line in a strong colour; others in grey.
- **Do not rely on colour alone** — label directly where possible, so colour-blind readers can follow.

Charts made in Sheets can be inserted into Docs and Slides and stay linked to the data.

## Key words

- **Line chart:** shows change over time
- **Bar chart:** compares categories by length
- **Axis:** the scale along the side or bottom of a chart
- **Data range:** the cells a chart is drawn from

- [Types of charts and graphs in Sheets](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/190718) — Google Docs Editors Help

Build a KPI dashboard for an NGGC centre.

**Deliverable:** A one-screen dashboard of five KPIs for a centre (attendance, new members, sessions held, budget used, feedback score).

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made

- Five KPIs with targets

## Understand it

A **KPI dashboard** is one screen that shows a manager how something is performing — without opening ten spreadsheets. **KPI** means **Key Performance Indicator**: a number that shows progress towards a goal.

**Choose few, meaningful KPIs.** For an NGGC centre, for example:

- **Attendance rate** — members present ÷ members expected.
- **Active members** — attended at least once this month.
- **New registrations** this month.
- **Dues collected** vs expected (%).
- **Lessons completed** or checks passed.

Five to seven KPIs is plenty. Each must have a **target** (e.g. attendance ≥ 75%) so the number means something.

**Structure the file:**

- **Data tabs** — raw records (attendance, payments), never edited by the dashboard.
- **Calculation tab** — formulas: `COUNTIF`, `SUMIF`, `COUNTIFS`, percentages.
- **Dashboard tab** — big numbers, charts and status colours only, all pulled by formula from the calculation tab.

**Design the dashboard:**

- **Big number tiles** at the top: the KPI, its target, and a status colour (conditional formatting: green on target, amber close, red off).
- **Trend charts** below — a line per KPI over recent weeks.
- **A date or filter cell** (e.g. month dropdown) that the formulas read, so one dashboard shows any month.
- **Last updated** date.

**Protect** the calculation and dashboard tabs. A dashboard that anyone can accidentally overwrite will soon show wrong numbers — and nobody will trust it.

## Key words

- **KPI:** Key Performance Indicator — a number showing progress to a goal
- **Target:** the value a KPI should reach
- **Dashboard:** a one-screen summary of KPIs
- **Status colour:** green/amber/red showing performance against target
