Looker Studio turns a sheet into an online report that updates itself. Add a **filter control** so the reader can explore. Where internet is limited, sketch the report from a prepared dataset.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Turn sample data into an interactive report, where available.

**Deliverable:** An interactive report connected to your Sheets data with a date filter and two charts. (Offline: a printed mock-up of the report.)

**With an AI assistant —** Ask an AI assistant which chart suits your question (trend → line, comparison → bar, share → pie). Then check the chart answers the question at a glance.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Connected to a Google Sheet
- At least one filter control
- Shared as view-only

## Understand it

**Looker Studio** (formerly Google Data Studio) is Google's free tool for turning data into **interactive reports** — dashboards where the reader can pick a date range, filter by centre, and hover for details. It reads directly from Google Sheets and many other sources, and the report updates when the data does.

**The workflow:**

1. **Prepare the data** in Google Sheets: one header row, one row per record, consistent columns, dates as real dates. Looker Studio is only as good as the table it reads.
2. Go to **lookerstudio.google.com** → *Blank report* → **Add data** → *Google Sheets* → choose the file and tab.
3. **Add charts** (*Add a chart*): **scorecards** for single KPIs, time series for trends, bar charts for comparisons, tables for detail.
4. For each chart, set the **dimension** (what you group by — date, centre, category) and the **metric** (what you measure — sum of sales, count of members).
5. **Add controls**: a **date range control** and a **dropdown filter** (e.g. centre), so readers explore the data themselves.
6. **Style** with a consistent theme; title every chart with its finding.
7. **Share** like a Google Doc — viewers can interact but not change the report.

**Dimension vs metric** is the key idea: dimensions are categories (text, dates); metrics are numbers that get added up, counted or averaged.

"Where available": Looker Studio needs internet and a Google account. If not available, the Sheets dashboard from week 20 achieves most of the same.

## Key words

- **Interactive report:** a report readers can filter and explore
- **Data source:** the table or system a report reads from
- **Dimension:** a category used to group data
- **Metric:** a number that is summed, counted or averaged

## Read and watch

- [Data Studio documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio) — Google Cloud
- [Data Studio overview](https://lookerstudio.google.com/) — Google

**Deliverable:** In Manager.io (or a provided equivalent): three invoices, five expenses and the resulting profit-and-loss summary.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain one bookkeeping term (invoice, receivable, expense). Check the explanation against the Manager.io guide — money records must follow the rules, not the chatbot.

## Understand it

Spreadsheets work for small businesses, but as transactions grow, **accounting software** keeps the books more reliably: every invoice, payment and expense is linked, and reports are produced automatically. **Manager.io** is free desktop accounting software (with paid cloud editions) used by many small businesses, including in Nigeria.

**Core ideas of bookkeeping** that the software applies:

- **Invoices (sales invoices)** — bills you send to customers: who, what, quantity, price, due date. An unpaid invoice is money owed to you (**accounts receivable**).
- **Receipts** — money coming in, linked to the invoice it pays.
- **Purchase invoices and payments** — bills from suppliers and the payments you make. Unpaid bills are what you owe (**accounts payable**).
- **Expenses** — categorised into **accounts** (Rent, Transport, Utilities…) — the **chart of accounts**.
- **Bank and cash accounts** — balances update automatically with each receipt and payment.

**Practising with simulated data:**

1. Set up a business (*Add business*), with the currency set to NGN.
2. Enable tabs: Customers, Sales Invoices, Receipts, Payments, Bank Accounts.
3. Create customers; issue three invoices; record a payment against one.
4. Record expenses through **Payments**, choosing the right account.
5. Look at **Reports**: Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, Aged Receivables (who owes, how long).

**Never use real business data for practice**, and keep login details private. Real books also need regular **backups**.

## Key words

- **Bookkeeping:** recording all financial transactions
- **Accounts receivable:** money customers owe you
- **Accounts payable:** money you owe suppliers
- **Chart of accounts:** the list of categories transactions are recorded under

> **Programme week 23 of 72 · Module 2: Spreadsheets, Finance and Business Intelligence.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

**Break-even** is the number of sales at which you stop losing money. Each unit contributes (price − variable cost) towards fixed costs. Pricing balances what customers will pay with what you need.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Perform break-even and pricing calculations.

**Deliverable:** A break-even sheet: fixed costs, variable cost per unit, price, break-even units and a price comparison.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost)
- Three price options compared
- A recommended price with a reason

## Understand it

**Break-even** answers the question every business must face: *how much must we sell before we stop losing money?* A spreadsheet makes it interactive — change a price and see the effect instantly.

**The inputs** (put each in its own labelled cell):

- **Selling price per unit** (B1)
- **Variable cost per unit** (B2) — materials, packaging, delivery per item.
- **Fixed costs per month** (B3) — rent, salaries, subscriptions.

**The calculations:**

- **Contribution per unit** = price − variable cost: `=B1-B2`
- **Break-even units** = fixed costs ÷ contribution: `=B3/(B1-B2)` — round **up** with `=ROUNDUP(B3/(B1-B2),0)`, because you cannot sell part of a unit.
- **Break-even revenue** = break-even units × price.
- **Margin of safety** = (expected sales − break-even sales) ÷ expected sales — how far sales can fall before losses begin.

**A profit table** for different sales levels: quantity in column A (0, 50, 100, 150…), revenue `=A6*$B$1`, total cost `=$B$3+A6*$B$2`, profit `=revenue−total cost`. A **line chart** of revenue and total cost shows the break-even point where the lines cross.

**Pricing scenarios:** copy the inputs into three columns — current price, +10%, −10% — and compare break-even. A lower price can need far more sales to break even.

Use **absolute references** (`$B$1`) so formulas copy correctly.

## Key words

- **Contribution:** price minus variable cost per unit
- **Break-even point:** sales at which total revenue equals total cost
- **Margin of safety:** how far sales can fall before a loss
- **Scenario:** a what-if version with different inputs

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Business](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpsvr82) — BBC Bitesize

## Today's tool

## Why it matters

Module 2's demonstration of mastery. Bring the numbers together into a story: **what happened, why, and what to do next** — and be ready to show the sheet behind every figure.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Present a simulated business's financial and operational performance.

**Deliverable:** A three-minute presentation of a simulated business's quarter: profit, cash, stock and KPIs, with one recommendation.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Uses the profit sheet, cashbook, inventory and dashboard
- Every number on a slide traces to a sheet
- One clear, evidenced recommendation

## Understand it

The Module 2 challenge asks you to act as a **business analyst**: take a simulated business's records and present how it is doing — financially and operationally — with evidence.

**What a strong presentation includes:**

1. **Headline finding first** — one sentence: "The business is profitable but cash is tight because customers pay late."
2. **Financial performance** — sales, gross and net profit, margins, trend over months (week 14); budget vs actual (week 16).
3. **Cash position** — reconciled cashbook (week 18); money owed to and by the business.
4. **Operations** — stock levels and reorder alerts (week 17); key KPIs against targets (week 20).
5. **Break-even and pricing** — how close the business is to break-even; effect of a price change (week 23).
6. **Recommendations** — two or three specific actions, each linked to the evidence: "Introduce a 5% discount for payment within 7 days, because ₦240,000 is currently over 30 days late."

**Evidence standards:**

- Every number **traceable** to a formula and source data.
- **Charts titled with findings**.
- **Honest limitations** — "The data covers only three months; seasonal effects are unknown."

**Delivery:** 5–7 minutes; slides with charts from Sheets; be ready for questions such as "How did you calculate that?" — open the sheet and show the formula.

The skill assessed is not producing numbers but **turning numbers into decisions**.

## Key words

- **Business analyst:** someone who turns data into recommendations
- **Traceable:** able to be followed back to its source
- **Limitation:** an honest statement of what the analysis cannot show

## Today's tool

**Google Forms**

## Why it matters

Businesses start from **problems people actually have**. Ask the people affected before building anything. Explain why you are asking and keep answers anonymous where you can.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Conduct a needs assessment for a real community problem.

**Deliverable:** A needs-assessment form about a real problem in your community, sent to at least 10 people with consent.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Problem stated clearly in the form's description
- Neutral questions, no personal data beyond what is needed
- At least 10 responses

## Understand it

Good businesses start from a **real problem** that real people have — not from an idea someone liked. A **needs assessment** finds out what a community actually needs, how badly, and what people do about it now.

**Define the problem area and the people.** "Young people in our area" is too broad. "Secondary-school students in Mushin who cannot afford private tutoring before WAEC" is something you can investigate.

**What to find out:**

- **Is the problem real and common?** How many people have it, and how often?
- **How painful is it?** What does it cost them — money, time, opportunity, health?
- **What do they do now?** Every problem already has some solution, even a poor one (an uncle who helps, a free YouTube channel). That is your competition.
- **What would they pay or do** to solve it — evidence of real demand, not polite interest.

**Designing the form (Google Forms):**

- Start with a short, honest **introduction**: who you are, why you are asking, how long it takes, how answers will be used.
- **Screening question** first, to confirm the person is in your target group.
- **Behaviour questions**: "In the last month, how many times did you…?"
- **Rating scales** for how serious each problem is.
- One or two **open questions**: "What is the hardest part of…?"
- **Under 10 questions.** Collect **no personal data you do not need**; for under-18s, follow your centre's consent rules.

A form alone is not enough — **talk to at least five people** in person as well. Conversations reveal what forms miss.

## Key words

- **Needs assessment:** research into what a community actually needs
- **Target group:** the specific people the problem affects
- **Screening question:** a question confirming someone is in the target group
- **Existing alternative:** what people currently do about the problem

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 26 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A **pivot table** summarises responses by category in seconds (Insert → Pivot table). Patterns are what most people said — note the surprises too.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Analyse customer responses and identify patterns.

**Deliverable:** An analysis of the needs assessment with counts, a chart and three patterns.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- COUNTIF or a pivot table used
- One chart of the main finding
- Three patterns written as evidence-based statements

## Understand it

Raw responses become insight when you find **patterns** — what many people say, what different groups say differently, and what surprises you.

**Clean the data first** (on a copy of the response sheet):

- Remove test responses and obvious duplicates.
- Standardise text answers ("Yaba", "yaba", "Yaba " → "Yaba") — *Data → Data cleanup → Trim whitespace* helps; Find and replace (Ctrl+H) fixes spellings.

**Quantitative answers (choices, scales):**

- **Counts and percentages** with `COUNTIF` — what share chose each option?
- **Averages** of rating questions — which problems are rated most serious?
- **Compare groups** with `COUNTIFS` or a **pivot table** (*Insert → Pivot table*): do JSS students answer differently from SSS students? Boys from girls? One area from another?

**Qualitative answers (open text) — code them:**

1. Read all the answers once.
2. Create **themes** (codes) as you notice them: "cost", "time", "no one to ask", "transport".
3. Add a column and tag each answer with its theme(s).
4. Count how many answers fall under each theme.
5. Keep two or three **direct quotes** that capture each theme in people's own words.

**State findings carefully:**

- Give the **number of respondents**: "23 of 40 (58%)…"
- Separate **what people said** from **what you conclude**.
- Note **who you did not reach** — a survey shared only on WhatsApp misses people without smartphones.

The output: three to five **key findings**, each backed by numbers and a quote.

## Key words

- **Pattern:** something that repeats across many responses
- **Coding (qualitative):** tagging open answers with themes
- **Respondent:** a person who answered the survey
- **Sampling bias:** results skewed by who was (or was not) asked

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 27 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**ChatGPT**

## Why it matters

An AI can suggest ideas quickly — but it does not know your community. Treat every answer as a **hypothesis** to test. Never paste respondents' personal details into an AI tool.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Generate business hypotheses and verify them against evidence.

**Deliverable:** Five business hypotheses generated with an AI assistant, each marked supported, not supported or untested against your survey data.

**With an AI assistant —** This week the AI is the tool. Write a clear prompt (role, task, context, format), get an answer, then **verify** it against evidence. Record what was right, what was wrong and how you checked.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- A prompt that gives role, task, context and format
- Each hypothesis checked against your data
- A note of anything the AI got wrong

## Understand it

A **business hypothesis** is a specific, testable belief that must be true for a business to work: "At least 30% of parents in our area would pay ₦5,000 a month for weekend coding classes." Entrepreneurs succeed by **testing** their riskiest hypotheses cheaply before investing money.

**Using ChatGPT (or a similar AI assistant) to generate hypotheses:** it is good at brainstorming — listing assumptions you have not thought of, suggesting customer segments, possible objections and alternative business models. A useful prompt gives context and asks for testable statements:

> "I'm planning weekend coding classes for 10–15-year-olds in Surulere, Lagos. List 10 assumptions that must be true for this to succeed, each written as a testable hypothesis with a number in it."

**Then verify each hypothesis against evidence — this is the real work:**

- The assistant **does not know your local market**. It may invent statistics, prices or "studies" that do not exist, and state them confidently. Treat every factual claim as **unverified**.
- For each hypothesis, ask: **what evidence would prove it wrong?** Then look for it — your needs-assessment data (weeks 1–2), interviews, market prices, official statistics.
- Mark each one: **Supported**, **Contradicted**, or **Untested**, with the evidence.

**Rank** hypotheses by **risk** — which, if wrong, would kill the business? Test those first.

**Responsible use:** never paste personal data from your survey into the assistant; say in your report where you used it; and keep the decisions yours.

## Key words

- **Hypothesis:** a specific, testable belief about the business
- **Assumption:** something believed true but not yet proven
- **Verification:** checking a claim against independent evidence
- **Riskiest assumption:** the belief that would sink the business if false

## Read and watch

- [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) — University of Helsinki
- [SIFT: the four moves](https://hapgood.us/2019/06/19/sift-the-four-moves/) — Mike Caulfield
- [Design thinking resources](https://dschool.stanford.edu/resources) — Stanford d.school

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

## This week's assignment

Generate business hypotheses and verify them against evidence. Five business hypotheses generated with an AI assistant, each marked supported, not supported or untested against your survey data.

**Today's session, to scale:**

> **Programme week 28 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Know who else serves your customer. A comparison table shows where you can be **better, cheaper or different** — and where you cannot compete.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Compare competitors, pricing and customer offerings.

**Deliverable:** A competitor comparison table of at least four competitors: price, product, location, strengths and weaknesses.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Four or more competitors
- Price comparison with average
- Your gap in the market in one sentence

## Understand it

Every business has competitors — including indirect ones and "doing nothing". Studying them shows what customers already get, what they pay, and where there is a **gap** you can fill.

**Identify competitors:**

- **Direct** — same product, same customers (another lesson centre nearby).
- **Indirect** — different product, same need (free YouTube tutorials, an older sibling who helps).
- **The status quo** — customers doing nothing, or doing it themselves.

**Build a comparison grid in Sheets** — one row per competitor, one column per factor:

| Competitor | Price | Location | Hours | Quality / features | Reviews / reputation | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Gather real data** — visit, call, check social media and reviews, ask customers. Note the date and source.
- Add **your own planned offer** as the last row, honestly.
- Use **conditional formatting** to highlight the best value in each column.

**Analyse:**

- **Price range** — `MIN`, `MAX`, `AVERAGE` of competitor prices; where would yours sit?
- **What everyone does** — the basics customers expect.
- **What no one does well** — the gap. Customer complaints in reviews are gold.
- **Your differentiation** — why would a customer choose you? Cheaper, closer, better quality, more convenient, more trusted? You cannot be best at everything; pick one or two.

A **positioning map** (a scatter chart with, say, price on one axis and quality on the other) shows where competitors cluster and where space is empty.

## Key words

- **Direct competitor:** offers the same product to the same customers
- **Indirect competitor:** meets the same need differently
- **Differentiation:** what makes your offer distinct
- **Positioning map:** a chart placing competitors on two key factors

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Business](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpsvr82) — BBC Bitesize

- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 20 Demonstration | 60 Guided hands-on practice | 25 Independent assignment | 15 Demonstration, feedback and submission
```

> **Programme week 29 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Canva**

## Why it matters

A **brand** is how people recognise and remember you. Keep it simple and consistent: one logo, two or three colours, two fonts. Check text contrast so everyone can read it.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a basic brand identity and product presentation.

**Deliverable:** A one-page brand sheet: name, logo, two colours, two fonts and a tagline, plus a product card.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Logo readable at small size
- Colours have good contrast
- Tagline under eight words

## Understand it

A **brand identity** is the consistent look and voice that makes a business recognisable and trusted: name, logo, colours, fonts, and the way it speaks. Consistency is the point — the same colours and style everywhere builds recognition.

**The elements:**

- **Logo** — simple enough to recognise at small sizes (a WhatsApp profile picture) and in one colour. Avoid fine details and too many colours.
- **Colour palette** — usually **one main colour**, one or two supporting colours, and neutrals (white, dark grey). Colours carry associations (green: fresh, natural; blue: trust; red: energy, urgency), but meaning varies by culture and context.
- **Typography** — **one or two fonts**: one for headings, one for body text. Readability beats decoration.
- **Tone of voice** — formal or friendly? Playful or serious? Write three adjectives and stick to them.
- **Imagery style** — real photos of your customers and products beat stock images.

**Accessibility:** text must contrast strongly with its background — at least **4.5:1** for normal text (check with a contrast checker). Light grey on white or yellow on white fails.

**A simple brand sheet** — one page showing the logo (and versions), colour codes (hex values like `#1B5E20`), fonts, and do's and don'ts — keeps everyone consistent.

**In Canva** (or any design tool): set up a **Brand Kit** with your logo, colours and fonts, then build the product presentation from a template using only those. Use only images and fonts you have the right to use.

## Key words

- **Brand identity:** the consistent visual and verbal style of a business
- **Colour palette:** the fixed set of brand colours
- **Hex code:** a code like #1B5E20 that specifies an exact colour
- **Tone of voice:** the personality in how a brand writes and speaks

## Read and watch

- [Branding](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/branding) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Colour theory](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/color-theory) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Contrast checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — WebAIM (Utah State University)
- [Choosing type](https://fonts.google.com/knowledge/choosing_type) — Google Fonts

- **If this is new to you:** follow the instructor's steps with the prepared sample data first, then repeat once on your own.
- **If you already can:** add one extra feature (a chart, a formula, an automation or a template) and teach it to a partner.
- **No internet?** Use the prepared offline dataset and an offline-compatible tool, or complete the exercise on paper and enter it at the next session.

> **Programme week 30 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Business Model Canvas**

## Why it matters

The **Business Model Canvas** shows a whole business on one page: who it serves, what value it gives, how it reaches them, and how money flows. Fill it with sticky notes so it is easy to change.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Map customers, value propositions, costs and revenue.

**Deliverable:** A completed Business Model Canvas (nine boxes) for your business idea.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to challenge your canvas: *"What is the weakest assumption here?"* Then decide what evidence would test it.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- All nine boxes filled
- Customer segment and value proposition clearly linked
- Costs and revenue streams realistic

## Understand it

The **Business Model Canvas**, created by Alexander Osterwalder and published by Strategyzer, describes how any business works on **one page**, in nine building blocks. It is used by start-ups, NGOs and large companies to think clearly and spot gaps.

**The nine blocks:**

1. **Customer segments** — who you serve (be specific; you may have more than one).
2. **Value propositions** — what problem you solve or need you meet for each segment, and why they would choose you.
3. **Channels** — how you reach and deliver to customers (WhatsApp, a shop, delivery riders, schools).
4. **Customer relationships** — how you win and keep customers (personal service, community, self-service).
5. **Revenue streams** — how money comes in (sales, subscriptions, fees, sponsorship) and how much.
6. **Key resources** — what you must have (equipment, space, skills, brand, data).
7. **Key activities** — what you must do well (cooking, teaching, marketing, deliveries).
8. **Key partners** — who helps you (suppliers, schools, a landlord, a payment provider).
9. **Cost structure** — the main costs, fixed and variable.

**How to use it:**

- Fill it with **sticky notes** (or a shared doc) so you can move and change items.
- Start with **customer segments and value propositions** — everything else depends on them.
- Check **fit**: does each value proposition match a segment's real need (weeks 1–2)? Do revenues cover costs (week 8)?
- Mark items that are **assumptions** (untested) differently from **facts** — they become the hypotheses to test (week 3).

The canvas changes as you learn; date each version.

## Key words

- **Business Model Canvas:** a one-page map of how a business works, in nine blocks
- **Value proposition:** the benefit a customer gets and why they would choose you
- **Customer segment:** a distinct group of customers
- **Revenue stream:** a way the business earns money

## Read and watch

- [The Business Model Canvas](https://www.strategyzer.com/library/the-business-model-canvas) — Strategyzer

> **Programme week 31 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Docs**

## Why it matters

A **business plan** explains how a business will work and why it will succeed. Write the summary last. Evidence from your research makes it believable.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Draft a business plan.

**Deliverable:** A 3–4 page business plan: summary, problem, solution, market, competition, operations, finance and next steps.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Uses headings and a table of contents
- Draws on your survey, competitor and canvas work
- Executive summary written last, placed first

## Understand it

A **business plan** explains what the business will do, how, and why it will succeed — for yourself, a partner, a bank, an investor or a grant panel. Writing it forces you to think through every part, and exposes gaps before they cost money.

**A practical structure:**

1. **Executive summary** (written last, placed first) — the whole plan in half a page: problem, solution, customers, money, the ask.
2. **The problem and the opportunity** — evidence from your needs assessment (weeks 1–2).
3. **The product or service** — what you offer and your value proposition.
4. **Market and customers** — who, how many, and what they currently use.
5. **Competition** — your comparison grid and differentiation (week 4).
6. **Marketing and sales** — how customers will find and buy from you.
7. **Operations** — location, equipment, suppliers, processes, who does what.
8. **Team** — who is involved and their relevant skills.
9. **Financial plan** — start-up costs, pricing, monthly costs, projected sales, break-even, cash flow (week 8).
10. **Risks** — the main risks and how you will handle them.
11. **The ask and milestones** — what you need and what you will achieve by when.

**Writing well:** short sections with headings (Docs styles → automatic **table of contents**: *Insert → Table of contents*); numbers instead of adjectives; evidence for every claim; plain language. **Separate facts from assumptions** — say which numbers are estimates.

A ten-page plan that is read beats a fifty-page plan that is not.

## Key words

- **Business plan:** a document explaining how a business will operate and succeed
- **Executive summary:** a short overview of the whole plan, placed first
- **Milestone:** a significant, dated achievement
- **Start-up costs:** one-off costs to launch the business

> **Programme week 32 of 72 · Module 3: Business Strategy and Entrepreneurship.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

Projections are educated guesses — **list your assumptions** so others can challenge them. Showing a worst case proves you have thought about risk.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Calculate costs, prices and projected margins.

**Deliverable:** A three-month projection: units, price, costs, margin and cash position.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Monthly projections with assumptions listed
- Margin per unit and total
- A best case and a worst case

## Understand it

The financial section of a business plan must answer three questions: **what does it cost to start, what will each sale earn, and when does it make money?**

**1. Start-up costs** — one-off: equipment, first stock, registration, deposit on premises, branding. List each with its real price and source.

**2. Unit economics** — for each product:

- **Variable cost per unit** (materials, packaging, delivery).
- **Price** — set by looking at three things: **cost** (price must be well above variable cost), **competitors** (week 4) and **value to the customer** (what they would pay).
- **Margin** per unit = price − variable cost; **margin %** = margin ÷ price.

**3. Monthly projection** — a sheet with months across the top (12 columns):

- **Projected units sold** — start modestly and grow; base it on evidence, not hope.
- **Revenue** = units × price.
- **Variable costs** = units × variable cost.
- **Fixed costs** — rent, salaries, data, etc.
- **Profit** = revenue − variable − fixed.
- **Cumulative profit** — when does it turn positive (recovering start-up costs)?

**Scenarios:** make **pessimistic, expected and optimistic** versions (copy the tab, change unit sales). If the business only works in the optimistic case, it is risky.

**Cash flow is different from profit:** customers may pay late, stock must be bought in advance. Add a simple cash row: cash in when actually received, cash out when actually paid.

Keep inputs in labelled cells at the top and use **absolute references**, so changing a price updates everything.

## Key words

- **Unit economics:** the revenue and costs of a single unit sold
- **Projection:** an estimate of future figures
- **Scenario analysis:** comparing pessimistic, expected and optimistic cases
- **Cash flow:** the timing of money actually coming in and going out

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Business](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpsvr82) — BBC Bitesize

## Today's tool

**Canva**

## Why it matters

Marketing tells the right people about your offer. Every piece needs **one message and one action** (call, visit, order). Only claim what is true.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Design marketing materials for the proposed business.

**Deliverable:** A flyer and two social-media posts for your business, using your brand sheet.

**With an AI assistant —** Try Canva's AI tools (Magic Write or text-to-image) for a first draft, then edit it so it is original, on-brand and honest. Do not use AI images of real people or logos you do not own.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Consistent with your brand colours and fonts
- One clear call to action
- Honest claims only

## Understand it

Marketing materials — flyers, social posts, posters, a WhatsApp catalogue — exist to make **a specific person** take **a specific action**. Design follows from that.

**Before designing, answer:**

- **Who** is it for? (Your customer segment.)
- **What should they do?** (Call, visit, order on WhatsApp, register.)
- **Where will they see it?** (A phone screen at arm's length; a poster across a street; a church noticeboard.)

**Principles of effective design:**

- **Visual hierarchy** — the most important thing is the biggest and most prominent: usually the **offer** or headline, then the image, then details, then the **call to action** and contact.
- **One message** — a flyer that says six things says nothing.
- **Benefit, not feature** — "Fresh lunch at your desk by 12:30" beats "We use quality ingredients."
- **Clear call to action** — "WhatsApp 0803 000 0000 to order" — big, and easy to act on.
- **Brand consistency** — your colours, fonts and logo from week 5.
- **White space** — empty space makes content readable.
- **Contrast** — text readable at a glance (4.5:1 minimum).
- **Right size for the platform** — square or 4:5 for feeds, 9:16 for Status and Stories, A5/A4 for print.

**Check before publishing:** spelling, phone number (call it!), prices, dates. Ask someone from the target group what they think it says and what they would do — if they cannot tell you in five seconds, simplify.

## Key words

- **Visual hierarchy:** arranging elements by importance
- **Call to action:** the instruction telling the reader what to do
- **White space:** empty space that improves readability
- **Benefit:** what the customer gains, rather than a product feature

## Read and watch

- [Visual hierarchy](https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/visual-hierarchy) — Interaction Design Foundation
- [Principles of visual design](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/principles-visual-design/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Contrast checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — WebAIM (Utah State University)

## Today's tool

**Google Slides**

## Why it matters

A pitch persuades someone to support you. Lead with the **problem**, show evidence, and end with a specific **ask**. Practise until you can pitch without reading.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Build an investor or stakeholder pitch deck.

**Deliverable:** A 7–10 slide pitch deck: problem, solution, market, business model, traction, team, finances, ask.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- A clear ask (amount or support needed)
- Evidence on every claim
- Delivered in under four minutes

## Understand it

A **pitch deck** is a short set of slides presented to investors, funders, partners or community stakeholders to win their support. It tells a story backed by evidence — in about **10 slides** and **5–10 minutes**.

**A standard sequence:**

1. **Title** — name, one-line description, presenter.
2. **Problem** — who has it and how badly, with evidence and a real example.
3. **Solution** — what you offer; a photo, demo or prototype.
4. **Market** — how many potential customers, and which segment you start with.
5. **Business model** — how you make money: price, costs, margin.
6. **Traction / validation** — evidence it works: survey results, test sales, sign-ups, partners.
7. **Competition** — your comparison and differentiation.
8. **Financials** — key projections and break-even (one chart).
9. **Team** — who and why they can deliver.
10. **The ask** — exactly what you want (₦ amount, space, partnership) and what it will achieve by when.

**Design:** one idea per slide; headline states the point; big numbers and charts instead of paragraphs; consistent brand theme; readable from the back.

**Stakeholder vs investor:** a community stakeholder (a school head, a local leader) cares more about **impact** and **safety**; an investor about **return** and **growth**. Adjust emphasis for the audience.

**Rehearse** with a timer, and prepare answers to the five hardest questions you can imagine. Keep a **backup slide** section with extra detail for questions.

## Key words

- **Pitch deck:** a short slide presentation seeking support
- **Traction:** evidence that customers want the product
- **Stakeholder:** anyone with an interest in the project
- **The ask:** exactly what you request from the audience

## Today's tool

**Google Forms + Sheets**

## Why it matters

Test before you build big. A **concept test** shows people the idea and asks if they would buy it and what would make it better. Listen to the negatives most.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Test a product concept and analyse feedback.

**Deliverable:** A concept test: a short form showing your product idea, at least 10 responses and a summary of what to change.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Concept clearly described or shown
- Likelihood-to-buy question on a scale
- Three changes you will make, from the feedback

## Understand it

Before investing heavily, test the **concept** with real potential customers. A **concept test** shows people a description, picture or prototype of the product and measures their reaction — and, more importantly, their **willingness to act**.

**What to show:** a short concept description (what it is, who it is for, the benefit, the price) plus a picture or simple prototype. Show the **real price** — interest without a price means little.

**What to measure (Google Forms):**

- **Clarity** — "In your own words, what is this?" (If they cannot say, the concept is unclear.)
- **Relevance** — "How much do you need something like this?" (1–5).
- **Purchase intent** — "How likely are you to buy it at ₦X?" (Definitely / Probably / Not sure / Probably not / Definitely not).
- **Price sensitivity** — "At what price would it be too expensive?"
- **Improvements** — "What would make it better?"
- **Commitment** — strongest evidence: "Leave your number if you want to be told when it launches" or a **pre-order**.

**Analysing in Sheets:**

- `COUNTIF` the answers to each option; percentages.
- Researchers often treat **only "Definitely"** answers as likely buyers — people overstate intent.
- Compare **segments** with a pivot table.
- Code the open answers into themes (week 2).

**Decide:** go ahead, **revise** the concept (and test again), or stop. All three are good outcomes — stopping a weak idea early saves money.

## Key words

- **Concept test:** testing reactions to a product idea before building it
- **Purchase intent:** how likely someone says they are to buy
- **Price sensitivity:** how demand changes with price
- **Pre-order:** a commitment to buy before launch — strong evidence

- [View and manage form responses](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/139706) — Google Docs Editors Help

## Why it matters

Module 3's demonstration of mastery. A **validated** concept is backed by evidence; a **revised** one changed because of it. Both are success — guessing is not.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

**Deliverable:** A final pitch of your concept with evidence of what you tested and changed.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made

## Success criteria

- Shows before-and-after from testing
- Financial projection included
- Answers questions from a panel

## Understand it

The Module 3 challenge asks you to present a business concept that has been **tested** — and either validated or honestly revised. Changing your idea because of evidence is a strength, not a failure.

**Tell the journey, with evidence:**

1. **The problem** — needs-assessment findings (weeks 1–2).
2. **Your hypotheses** — what you assumed (week 3) and **what the evidence showed** for each: supported, contradicted, untested.
3. **The market** — competitors and your differentiation (week 4).
4. **The business model** — your canvas (week 6), with assumptions marked.
5. **The numbers** — costs, price, margin, break-even, scenarios (week 8).
6. **Concept test results** (week 11) — what customers said and did.
7. **What changed** — "We dropped weekday classes because only 3 of 40 could attend; we added a sibling discount because cost was the top barrier."
8. **Brand and marketing** samples (weeks 5, 9).
9. **Next steps** — the riskiest remaining assumption and how you will test it.

**Validated** means the key hypotheses have evidence from real potential customers — not that everyone liked it.

**Present** with your pitch deck (week 10), 7–10 minutes, then questions. Assessors look for **honesty about evidence**, clear reasoning from findings to decisions, and realistic numbers.

Keep all your materials in the project folder; they become the foundation of the Year 3 capstone.

## Key words

- **Validated:** supported by evidence from real potential customers
- **Pivot (business):** changing direction based on evidence
- **Iteration:** improving through repeated test-and-change cycles

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a project board with tasks, owners and deadlines.

**Deliverable:** A Trello board for a real or simulated project with lists To do, Doing, Done and at least 12 cards.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Every card has an owner and a due date
- Labels for task type
- Shared with the team

## Understand it

A **project** is temporary work with a defined goal, a start and an end — an event, a product launch, a fundraising drive. Project management makes sure everyone knows **what** must be done, **by whom**, and **by when**, and can see progress at a glance.

**Trello** organises work as a **Kanban board**:

- **Board** — the whole project ("Centre Open Day").
- **Lists** — columns showing stages, typically **To do → Doing → Done** (add "Waiting" or "Review" if useful).
- **Cards** — individual tasks ("Book the hall", "Print 200 flyers"). Cards move across lists as work progresses.

**On each card:**

- A **clear title** starting with a verb.
- **Members** — the **owner** (one person responsible, even if others help).
- **Due date**.
- **Description** — what "done" means.
- **Checklist** for sub-steps.
- **Labels** — colours for categories (Venue, Marketing, Budget) or priority.
- **Attachments** and comments — keep discussion on the card, not scattered in chats.

**Kanban principles:**

- **Visualise the work** — everything on the board.
- **Limit work in progress** — too many cards in "Doing" means nothing finishes.
- **Pull, don't push** — people take the next card when they finish one.

**Habits:** update the board as work happens; review it together weekly. A board that is not updated becomes a fiction.

## Key words

- **Project:** temporary work with a defined goal, start and end
- **Kanban board:** a board of columns showing work stages
- **Card:** a single task on the board
- **Work in progress (WIP):** tasks currently being worked on

**Trello**

## Why it matters

A **milestone** is a point of progress; a **deliverable** is the thing you produce. Break big work into pieces small enough to finish in a week.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Break a project into milestones and deliverables.

**Deliverable:** A project broken into four milestones, each with its deliverables as checklists.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made

- Four milestones with dates

## Understand it

Big projects feel overwhelming until they are broken down. Two ideas help: **milestones** and **deliverables**.

- A **deliverable** is a **tangible output** — something you can see, hand over or check: a printed programme, a booked venue (with a receipt), a registration form, a final report.
- A **milestone** is a **significant point in time** — usually when a key deliverable is complete or a phase ends: "Venue confirmed (7 March)", "Registrations open (10 March)", "Event day (28 March)". Milestones have no duration; they mark progress.

**Breaking the project down (a work breakdown structure):**

1. Start with the **final goal**.
2. Split into **phases** or major deliverables (Venue, Programme, Marketing, Logistics, Budget).
3. Split each into **tasks** small enough to assign to one person and complete in a few days.
4. Identify **dependencies** — what must finish before something else can start (you cannot print flyers before the date is confirmed).

**In Trello:**

- Create a **list per phase**, or use **labels** for phases.
- Make **milestone cards** with a distinctive label (e.g. purple "MILESTONE") and due dates.
- Under each, task cards with owners and due dates; **checklists** for sub-steps.
- Use the **Calendar** or **Timeline** view (where available) to see dates.

Define **"done"** for each deliverable (acceptance criteria) — "Flyer approved by the coordinator and 200 copies printed" — so there is no argument about whether it is finished.

## Key words

- **Deliverable:** a tangible output of a project
- **Milestone:** a key point in time marking progress
- **Work breakdown structure:** a project split into phases and tasks
- **Dependency:** a task that must finish before another can start

- [Trello 101](https://trello.com/guide/trello-101) — Trello

## Today's tool

## Why it matters

Turn the plan into time. A recurring check-in keeps a team in sync; reminders stop deadlines sneaking up.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Schedule project activities and reminders.

**Deliverable:** A project calendar linked to your milestones, with team meetings and reminders.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to list the steps of your project in order, then check each date is realistic for your team before it goes in the calendar.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Milestones on the calendar
- Recurring weekly check-in
- Reminders on deadlines

## Understand it

A Trello board says **what** must be done; a **calendar** makes **when** visible to everyone and sends reminders so nothing depends on memory.

**Turning the plan into a schedule:**

1. List the **milestones** with their dates (week 14).
2. **Work backwards** from each: if invitations must go by 14 March and printing takes 3 days, the design must be approved by 10 March.
3. Add **buffer** — tasks almost always take longer than expected. A day or two of slack before key milestones absorbs delays.
4. Watch the **critical path** — the chain of dependent tasks with no slack. Any delay there delays the whole project.

**In Google Calendar:**

- Create a **dedicated project calendar** (*Other calendars → + → Create new calendar*) and **share** it with the team (*Settings and sharing → Share with specific people*).
- **Milestones** as all-day events with a clear title and owner: "MILESTONE: Venue confirmed — Ada".
- **Task deadlines** as all-day events; **meetings** as timed events with an agenda link in the description.
- **Notifications** — e.g. 3 days and 1 day before deadlines.
- **Recurring** weekly project check-in meetings.
- Use **colours** to distinguish milestones, deadlines and meetings.

**Keep Trello and Calendar consistent** — when a due date changes on a card, change the calendar too (or use Trello's calendar features). Two plans that disagree are worse than one.

Review the schedule weekly and **re-plan** honestly when things slip.

## Key words

- **Schedule:** the plan of when each task and milestone happens
- **Buffer (slack):** spare time built in to absorb delays
- **Critical path:** the chain of dependent tasks that sets the project's end date

## Today's tool

**Google Docs**

## Why it matters

Meetings without agendas waste time; meetings without **action points** change nothing. Minutes record decisions and who does what by when.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Prepare meeting agendas, minutes and action points.

**Deliverable:** An agenda for a team meeting and the minutes after it, with an action table (action, owner, date).

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Agenda sent before the meeting
- Minutes record decisions, not every word
- Action table complete

## Understand it

Meetings are expensive — six people for an hour is six hours of work. **Agendas**, **minutes** and **action points** make them worth it.

**The agenda** (sent at least a day before):

- **Purpose** — what the meeting must decide or achieve.
- **Date, time, place/link, attendees**.
- **Items**, each with an owner and time: "1. Venue options — Tunde — 10 min (decision needed)".
- **Papers to read beforehand**, linked.

A meeting without a purpose should be an email.

**Minutes** — the official record:

- Date, attendees, apologies (who was absent).
- For each item: a **brief summary** of discussion (not a transcript), the **decision** made, and **actions**.
- Approved at the next meeting as accurate.

**Action points** — the most important part:

| Action | Owner | Due date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confirm venue booking and pay deposit | Tunde | 7 March | Open |

Every action needs **one named owner** and a **date**. "We will look into it" is not an action.

**In Google Docs:**

- Create a **template** (agenda + minutes + action table) and copy it for each meeting.
- Use **@mentions** to assign actions — owners get notified, and the action appears as an assigned comment.
- Store in the project folder, named by date: `2026-03-05_meeting-minutes`.

Start the next meeting by **reviewing the action points** from the last one.

## Key words

- **Agenda:** the list of items a meeting will cover
- **Minutes:** the official record of a meeting
- **Action point:** a task from a meeting with an owner and date
- **Apologies:** people who sent notice they could not attend

> **Programme week 41 of 72 · Module 4: Project Management and Administration.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Google Drive**

## Why it matters

Control means the right people can find and change the right files. Set **permissions by role**, write the rules down, and archive rather than delete.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Establish a controlled digital filing system.

**Deliverable:** A controlled filing system with permissions, naming rules and a one-page filing guide.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Folder permissions set by role
- Naming convention written down
- Archive folder for old versions

## Understand it

A **controlled** filing system goes beyond tidy folders: it decides **who can see and change what**, keeps **one authoritative version** of each document, and makes sure nothing important is lost or leaked.

**Elements of control:**

1. **Structure and naming rules** (from Module 1) — numbered folders, date-first file names, documented in a README.
2. **Access by role**:
   - Share **folders**, not individual files, with the right people.
   - **Least privilege** — viewers by default; editors only where needed; restrict who can re-share (*Share → settings gear → Editors can change permissions and share* — untick).
   - Keep **sensitive** material (personal data, finance, HR) in a separate restricted folder.
3. **Version control**:
   - Work in **one living document**, not copies. Google Docs keeps **version history** — name key versions (*File → Version history → Name current version*: "Approved 14 March").
   - For files that must be frozen (signed contracts, approved budgets), save a **PDF** in an `Approved` subfolder.
4. **Ownership** — each folder has an **owner** responsible for its organisation. Use a **shared drive** (where available) so files belong to the organisation, not to a person's account — when someone leaves, the files stay.
5. **Archiving and retention** — move finished projects to `99 Archive`; delete personal data when it is no longer needed.
6. **Backup** — critical documents also stored elsewhere.

**Audit** access regularly: who still has access who should not?

## Key words

- **Access control:** deciding who can view or change files
- **Least privilege:** giving people only the access they need
- **Authoritative version:** the single official copy of a document
- **Retention:** how long records are kept before deletion

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

A tracker shows whether the project is on time. Use **data validation** for status and a formula for % complete. Red items need action this week.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a project tracker and progress dashboard.

**Deliverable:** A tracker of tasks with status, % complete and a progress chart.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Status drop-down for every task
- Overall % complete calculated
- Progress chart on a dashboard tab

## Understand it

A **project tracker** in Sheets gives a structured, calculable view of progress — and a **dashboard** summarises it for managers who do not want to read every row.

**The tracker (one row per task):**

| Task | Phase | Owner | Start | Due | Status | % complete | Days late |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Status** as a dropdown (*Data → Data validation*): Not started / In progress / Blocked / Done.
- **Days late**: `=IF(AND(F2<>"Done", TODAY()>E2), TODAY()-E2, 0)` — counts days past the due date for unfinished tasks.
- **Conditional formatting**: Blocked = red, Done = green, overdue rows highlighted.
- **Checkboxes** (*Insert → Checkbox*) are an alternative for simple done/not done.

**The dashboard tab:**

- **Overall progress**: `=COUNTIF(F:F,"Done")/COUNTA(A2:A)` formatted as %.
- **Tasks by status**: `COUNTIF` for each status, with a bar or pie chart.
- **Overdue tasks**: `=COUNTIF(H:H,">0")`.
- **By owner**: `COUNTIFS` of open tasks per person — reveals overload.
- **By phase**: progress per phase.
- **Next milestones** with dates.

**A simple RAG status** for the whole project — **Red** (in serious trouble), **Amber** (at risk), **Green** (on track) — agreed by clear rules (e.g. Red if a milestone will be missed).

Update it at a fixed time each week; a tracker is only as good as its last update.

## Key words

- **Project tracker:** a structured list of tasks with status and dates
- **RAG status:** Red/Amber/Green summary of project health
- **Overdue:** past the due date and not done
- **TODAY():** a function that returns the current date

> **Programme week 43 of 72 · Module 4: Project Management and Administration.** Every Saturday: open a tool, perform a task, produce an output, demonstrate what you learnt.

## Today's tool

**Draw.io**

## Why it matters

A **process map** shows how work actually flows. Diamonds are decisions. Mapping reveals delays and duplicated steps you can remove.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Map a business process visually.

**Deliverable:** A flowchart of one real process (e.g. registering a new member) with start, steps, decisions and end.

**With an AI assistant —** ask it to list the steps of a process in order, then draw it yourself and check it with someone who does the job.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Standard shapes (oval, rectangle, diamond)
- Every decision has yes and no paths
- Checked with someone who does the process

## Understand it

A **process map** (flowchart) shows how work flows through a business: the steps, the decisions, and who does each part. Drawing it often reveals delays, duplicated work and gaps that nobody noticed in words.

**Standard shapes:**

- **Oval** — start and end ("Customer sends order", "Order delivered").
- **Rectangle** — a step or task ("Check stock").
- **Diamond** — a decision with yes/no branches ("In stock?").
- **Parallelogram** — input or output (a form, an invoice).
- **Arrows** — the direction of flow.

**Swimlanes** — horizontal (or vertical) bands, one per person or department (Customer, Sales, Store, Delivery). Each step sits in the lane of whoever does it. Swimlanes show **hand-offs** — where work passes between people — which is where most delays and mistakes happen.

**Drawing it in draw.io (diagrams.net)** — free, works in the browser and saves to Google Drive or your device:

1. Open draw.io, choose where to save, start a blank diagram (or the flowchart template).
2. Drag shapes from the left panel; connect them by hovering and dragging the blue arrows.
3. Double-click a shape to type its label — start with a verb.
4. Use *Arrange → Align/Distribute* to keep it tidy.
5. Export as PNG or PDF (*File → Export as*).

**Map the process as it really is** ("as-is") by watching and asking the people who do it — not as you think it is. Then mark problems (delays, rework, unclear decisions) and draw an improved **"to-be"** version.

## Key words

- **Process map:** a diagram of the steps and decisions in a process
- **Swimlane:** a band showing which person or team does each step
- **Hand-off:** where work passes from one person to another
- **As-is / to-be:** the current process / the improved one

## Read and watch

- [Flowcharts and process mapping](https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/process-mapping) — Atlassian
- [draw.io documentation](https://www.drawio.com/docs) — draw.io

## Today's tool

**Google Docs**

## Why it matters

An **SOP** lets anyone do a task correctly, every time. Test it by asking someone else to follow it — where they get stuck is where it is unclear.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Write a standard operating procedure.

**Deliverable:** An SOP for the process you mapped: purpose, scope, roles, numbered steps and checks.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Numbered steps anyone could follow
- Roles and responsibilities clear
- Tested by someone who did not write it

## Understand it

A **standard operating procedure (SOP)** is a written, step-by-step instruction for a routine task, so that **anyone** trained can do it the same way, to the same standard. SOPs make quality consistent, make training faster, and let the business run when key people are away.

**A good SOP contains:**

- **Title** and **SOP number**, **version** and **date**, **owner** (who keeps it up to date), and who approved it.
- **Purpose** — why the procedure exists.
- **Scope** — when it applies and to whom.
- **Responsibilities** — who does what.
- **Materials / tools / access needed**.
- **Procedure** — numbered steps, each starting with an **action verb** ("Open", "Check", "Record"). One action per step. Include **decision points**: "If the amount is over ₦50,000, get the coordinator's approval before paying."
- **Safety or quality checks** and what to do if something goes wrong.
- **Records** produced (forms, logs).
- **Related documents** and the **process map** (week 19).

**Writing well:** plain language; short steps; screenshots or photos where they help; written for someone new. Avoid "as usual" or "the normal way".

**Test it:** give it to someone who has never done the task and **watch them follow it** without help. Every hesitation or question is a gap — fix it.

**Control:** keep SOPs in a controlled folder, update the version when anything changes, and review them at least once a year.

## Key words

- **SOP:** standard operating procedure — written instructions for a routine task
- **Version control:** tracking changes with version numbers and dates
- **Process owner:** the person responsible for keeping a procedure current

## Read and watch

- [SOP: what it is and how to create one](https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/knowledge-sharing/documentation/standard-operating-procedures) — Atlassian

## Today's tool

**Google Sheets**

## Why it matters

**Procurement** is buying properly: compare quotes, get approval, record receipt. Good records protect the organisation's money and people's trust.

## Demonstration (20 minutes)

- The instructor shows the tool live: where to find it, the three or four actions today's task needs, and one common mistake
- Learners follow on their own device (or watch on the shared screen where devices are limited)

## Guided hands-on practice (60 minutes)

- Work through the task together on the prepared sample data, step by step
- Pairs check each other's work against the success criteria below
- The instructor circulates: everyone must have done each step themselves

## Independent assignment (25 minutes)

Create a procurement and stock register.

**Deliverable:** A procurement register: request, supplier, quote, approval, received and stock updated.

## Demonstration, feedback and submission (15 minutes)

- Each learner shows their output and explains one decision they made
- One piece of feedback from a peer or the instructor
- Submit the link or file in the member portal before leaving

## Success criteria

- Every purchase has an approval step
- Three quotes compared for one item
- Stock register updated on receipt

## Understand it

**Procurement** is how an organisation buys goods and services — fairly, at good value, and with records that show where every naira went. Weak procurement is one of the commonest routes for waste and fraud.

**A basic procurement process:**

1. **Request** — someone states what is needed, why, how many, and the budget line.
2. **Approval** — an authorised person approves before money is committed (with limits: e.g. above ₦50,000 needs a second approval).
3. **Quotes** — for larger purchases, get **at least three quotes** from different suppliers, and record them.
4. **Selection** — choose on value (price, quality, reliability, delivery), and record **why**.
5. **Purchase order / payment** — pay the supplier, keep the **invoice and receipt**.
6. **Receipt of goods** — someone **other than the buyer** checks the delivery against the order (quantity, quality) and signs.
7. **Record** in the stock register.

**Separation of duties** — the person who requests, approves, pays and receives should not all be one person. This is a basic **internal control**.

**The register in Sheets:**

- **Procurement log**: Date, Item, Requested by, Approved by, Supplier, Quotes obtained, Amount, Invoice no., Received by, Date received.
- **Stock register**: Item, Opening, Received (linked to procurement), Issued, Balance, Reorder level.
- Use **SUMIF** to total spending by budget line, and compare with the budget.

Keep scanned receipts linked in the log (a Drive link column). An auditor should be able to trace any purchase from request to receipt.

## Key words

- **Procurement:** the process of buying goods and services
- **Quotation:** a supplier's stated price for specified goods
- **Separation of duties:** dividing tasks so no one person controls a whole transaction
- **Audit trail:** records that let every transaction be traced
